title: Humanitarian Collapse: Disregarding the Best Interests of the Child
subtitle: Serbian justice has demonstrated a total blindness to the fate of children. No authority — from the courts to the Asylum Office — has conducted the mandatory proportionality test.
intro: The right to family life (Article 8 ECHR) is not a decorative norm. In extradition cases, it imposes an imperative duty on the state: to assess the 'best interests of the child'. In the Lagovsky case, Serbia chose the path of absolute formalism, effectively excluding children from the legal framework and ignoring the risk of family destruction as a humanitarian disaster.

family_block.title: The Facts: Hostages of the Procedure
family_block.intro: This is a documentary record of the family's deep integration into Serbian society, which the authorities preferred not to notice.

facts.label: Deep Integration of Children in Serbia
facts.text: Aleksei (13) and Ilya (15) have lived in Belgrade for over three years. They don't just attend school; they are integrated socially, culturally, and linguistically. For them, their father's extradition means not just separation, but the collapse of their entire living environment.

facts.label: Economic Vulnerability
facts.text: The family lives solely on the mother's income (a nurse). Lagovsky's extradition and his detention in the RF would condemn the family in Serbia to extreme poverty and deprive the children of basic support.

facts.label: Good Faith Relocation
facts.text: The family moved to Serbia legally in 2023, long before Lagovsky became aware of the fabricated case. Serbia has become their new home, not a temporary refuge.

facts.label: Risk of Family Separation
facts.text: Transferring Lagovsky to Russia would lead to a prolonged separation from his two minor children and wife. The children have no basis or realistic ability to follow their father to Russia — a country the family left for safety reasons.

echr_block.title: Legal Standard: What Serbia Was Obliged to Do

paras.text: According to Jeunesse v. the Netherlands (2014), the interests of minor children are of paramount importance. A state cannot simply extradite a parent without assessing whether the children can follow them and what damage this will cause to their development.
In Othman v. UK (2012), it is emphasized: extradition cannot be carried out 'in a vacuum'. It must take into account all Convention risks, including the destruction of family life.

The 'Boultif criteria' (Boultif v. Switzerland, 2001) require the court to weigh the severity of the charge against the interests of the family. In the Lagovsky case, where the charge is refuted by arbitration courts, the balance of Article 8 ECHR tips unconditionally.

failure_title: Chronicle of Inaction: Total Failure of Assessment
failure_desc: Four levels of the Serbian system ignored Article 8 ECHR. This is a systemic violation of the Republic of Serbia's Convention obligations.

failures.title: Higher Court of Belgrade: Procedural Blindness
failures.what_happened: The court limited itself to checking stamps on documents from Moscow. The fact that two minor children are fully integrated in Serbia was not even mentioned in the decision. The court abdicated its role as a human rights defender, becoming a purely technical body.
failures.what_missing: Total absence of any mention of Article 8 ECHR or the children's interests.
failures.why_matters: The first instance is the foundation of justice. If it ignores the humanitarian dimension, the entire subsequent procedure is flawed.

failures.title: Court of Appeal: Silent Endorsement
failures.what_happened: Despite the defense's detailed arguments regarding the family's integration, the Court of Appeal chose to remain silent. In international law, a court's silence on a key defense argument is equated to a denial of justice.
failures.what_missing: Assessment of the proportionality of the interference with family life.
failures.why_matters: The Appeal is the last judicial filter before a political decision. Its failure to consider Article 8 makes Serbia responsible for the subsequent violation of the Convention.

failures.title: Supreme Court: Retreat into Formalism
failures.what_happened: The Supreme Court categorized the family life arguments as 'questions of fact' not subject to review. This is a legal subversion: the applicability of Article 8 ECHR is a fundamental question of law.
failures.what_missing: Legal qualification of the family situation through the lens of the ECHR.
failures.why_matters: When a country's highest court refuses to protect the Constitution and the Convention by citing formalities, it means a paralysis of the human rights protection system.

failures.title: Asylum Commission: Ignoring Humanitarian Risks
failures.what_happened: The asylum authorities formally cited the absence of 'Convention grounds for persecution,' completely ignoring the standalone humanitarian threat of violating Article 8 ECHR through family separation.
failures.what_missing: Analysis of the risk of inhuman treatment in the context of the minor children's interests.
failures.why_matters: The asylum procedure should have been a safeguard, but it turned into a mechanism for legitimizing formal refusals.

proportionality_block.title: Proportionality Test: A Failed Exam
proportionality_block.intro: Interference with family life is only justified if a balance is struck. In the Lagovsky case, this balance is entirely absent.

items.assessment: The aim of extradition is punishment for fraud. But the transaction was recognized as lawful by the arbitration courts of the RF. Prosecution for a lawful act cannot be a legitimate aim for destroying a family.

The extradition of an external consultant in a case where the main participants received suspended sentences is not 'necessary'. Destroying the lives of two children for the sake of a formal surrender in an economic dispute is an act of cruelty, not justice.

On one side of the scale is a formal request regarding a civil dispute. On the other are the fates of two teenagers, a long-term separation from their father, and the economic collapse of the family. Serbia hasn't even tried to weigh these factors.

serbia_obligation.title: Serbia's Responsibility
serbia_obligation.text: By extraditing Lagovsky, Serbia knowingly sends him into a jurisdiction where ECtHR mechanisms no longer apply. This means Serbia assumes full responsibility for the consequences of family separation. The lack of Article 8 assessment in national decisions is a documented failure to fulfill international obligations.

conclusion_title: Outcome: The Right to Protection Remains Unfulfilled
conclusion_paras: The systemic ignoring of Article 8 ECHR by Serbian authorities is not an error but a conscious choice in favor of formalism over humanity.

International standards (Boultif, Üner, Jeunesse cases) prohibit extradition without a detailed humanitarian analysis. The fact that the interests of Aleksei and Ilya Lagovsky are entirely absent from the Serbian court decisions makes the extradition illegal under European law.

The last chance to correct this violation rests with the Administrative Court of Serbia. Continued disregard will lead to an inevitable appeal to international bodies against the Republic of Serbia itself.
summary: The Serbian legal system completely ignored the interests of Dmitry Lagovsky's two minor children. The lack of assessment under Article 8 ECHR (the right to family life) in all judicial acts is a gross violation of Serbia's international obligations and makes the extradition an act of arbitrariness.
